expectedText:
RIGHT TO A DAY OF REST — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Jordan Lee · Acme, Inc.

PURPOSE
Acme, Inc. provides this information sheet to Jordan Lee to describe the California statutory right to a day of rest set out in Labor Code sections 550 through 558.1, including the core one-day-rest-in-seven provisions, the statutory exceptions to those provisions, and how California's courts have construed them. This information sheet states general rules of California law. It is not a statement of Acme, Inc.'s scheduling practices, and it does not describe what any particular schedule for Jordan Lee does or should look like.

ENTITLEMENT TO ONE DAY'S REST IN SEVEN
California law entitles every person employed in any occupation of labor to one day's rest in seven. This entitlement is stated as a right belonging to the employee, distinct from the separate statutory prohibition on an employer causing an employee to work more than six days in seven.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-03]
  "Every person employed in any occupation of labor is entitled to one day's rest therefrom in seven."
  — Cal. Lab. Code § 551 (leginfo.legislature.ca.gov text), California Labor Code, Division 2, Part 2, Chapter 1 (General), day of rest entitlement (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?sectionNum=551.&lawCode=LAB)
  Known gap: This is California law. Section 551 states the entitlement in the passive voice, from the employee's perspective ("is entitled to"), without itself defining "one day's rest," specifying how the seven-day period is measured, or prescribing a remedy for its own violation; the companion clause in this information sheet describing the California Supreme Court's construction in Mendoza v. Nordstrom addresses how the seven-day period is measured. Section 551 does not by its own terms distinguish exempt from non-exempt employees; the separate exceptions described in this information sheet (Labor Code §§ 554, 556) apply to both section 551 and section 552 alike.

PROHIBITION ON CAUSING MORE THAN SIX DAYS' WORK IN SEVEN
California law separately prohibits an employer from causing its employees to work more than six days in seven. This provision is framed as a duty on the employer, addressed to what the employer causes, rather than solely as a right the employee may waive or decline to exercise. A companion clause in this information sheet describes how the California Supreme Court has construed what it means for an employer to "cause" an employee to go without a day of rest.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-03]
  "No employer of labor shall cause his employees to work more than six days in seven."
  — Cal. Lab. Code § 552 (leginfo.legislature.ca.gov text), California Labor Code, Division 2, Part 2, Chapter 1 (General), prohibition on employer causing excess work (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?sectionNum=552.&lawCode=LAB)
  Known gap: This is California law. Section 552, standing alone, does not define the word "cause"; the companion Mendoza v. Nordstrom clause in this information sheet addresses that construction question, drawn from a different, independent source (a California Supreme Court opinion) rather than from the statutory text itself. Section 552 and section 551 are both part of the same statutory chapter (Labor Code §§ 550-558.1) and are not independent sources of each other, though they are independently numbered sections addressing distinct legal questions (an employee entitlement versus an employer prohibition).

EXCEPTION FOR SHORT TOTAL WEEKLY OR DAILY HOURS
Sections 551 and 552 do not apply to any employer or employee when the total hours of employment do not exceed 30 hours in any week or six hours in any one day of that week. A companion clause in this information sheet describes the California Supreme Court's construction of how this exception applies across the days of a single week.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-03]
  "Sections 551 and 552 shall not apply to any employer or employee when the total hours of employment do not exceed 30 hours in any week or six hours in any one day thereof."
  — Cal. Lab. Code § 556 (leginfo.legislature.ca.gov text), California Labor Code, Division 2, Part 2, Chapter 1 (General), exception for short total hours (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?sectionNum=556.&lawCode=LAB)
  Known gap: This is California law. Section 556 is written as an exception to sections 551 and 552 specifically, and its own text does not state whether the six-hours-in-any-one-day language means no single day may exceed six hours, or whether at least one qualifying day is enough; the companion Mendoza v. Nordstrom clause addresses that construction question using a separate, independent source (a California Supreme Court opinion), not the statutory text of section 556 itself. Section 556 does not state a total combined weekly-hours-and-daily-hours test beyond the "30 hours in any week or six hours in any one day" language quoted here.

EMERGENCY, ACCUMULATION, AND COLLECTIVE-BARGAINING EXCEPTIONS
California law provides further exceptions to sections 551 and 552 beyond the short-total-hours exception. Sections 551 and 552 do not apply to cases of emergency, to work performed in the protection of life or property from loss or destruction, or to any common carrier engaged in or connected with the movement of trains. Separately, the statute permits an accumulation of days of rest when the nature of the employment reasonably requires that an employee work seven or more consecutive days, provided the employee receives, within each calendar month, days of rest equivalent to one day's rest in seven; where a valid collective bargaining agreement addresses hours of work, the equivalent-one-day-in-seven requirement applies notwithstanding other provisions of this chapter relating to such agreements, unless the agreement expressly provides otherwise. The Chief of the Division of Labor Standards Enforcement may also exempt an employer or employees from sections 551 and 552 upon a judgment that hardship will result.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-03]
  "Sections 551 and 552 do not apply to cases of emergency or to work performed in the protection of life or property from loss or destruction, or to any common carrier engaged in or connected with the movement of trains. Nothing in this chapter shall be construed to prevent an accumulation of days of rest when the nature of the employment reasonably requires that the employee work seven or more consecutive days, if in each calendar month the employee receives days of rest equivalent to one day's rest in seven."
  — Cal. Lab. Code § 554(a) (leginfo.legislature.ca.gov text), California Labor Code, Division 2, Part 2, Chapter 1 (General), emergency and accumulation exceptions (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?sectionNum=554.&lawCode=LAB)
  "In addition to the exceptions specified in subdivision (a), the Chief of the Division of Labor Standards Enforcement may, when in his or her judgment hardship will result, exempt any employer or employees from the provisions of Sections 551 and 552."
  — Cal. Lab. Code § 554(b) (leginfo.legislature.ca.gov text), California Labor Code, Division 2, Part 2, Chapter 1 (General), hardship exemption authority (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?sectionNum=554.&lawCode=LAB)
  Known gap: This is California law, drawn from Labor Code section 554, a separate and independently numbered section from sections 551, 552, and 556 discussed in this information sheet's other authority clauses, though it is part of the same statutory chapter and cross-references sections 551 and 552 directly rather than standing wholly apart from them. Section 554 does not itself define "emergency," "case of emergency," or what makes a hardship determination proper; it commits the hardship-exemption judgment to the Chief of the Division of Labor Standards Enforcement without stating a further standard in the statutory text quoted here. This clause does not address whether any particular employer or employee circumstance falls within these exceptions.

MENDOZA V. NORDSTROM: HOW THE RIGHT IS MEASURED
The California Supreme Court, answering questions certified to it by the Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals, construed the day-of-rest statutes in three respects. First, the one-day's-rest-in-seven guarantee is measured by the workweek, not by any rolling period of seven consecutive days; a period of more than six consecutive days of work that stretches across more than one workweek is not automatically prohibited on that basis alone. Second, the section 556 exception for short daily hours applies only to an employee who never exceeds six hours of work on any day of the workweek; if an employee works more than six hours on even one day of the week, a day of rest must be provided during that workweek, subject to whatever other exceptions might otherwise apply. Third, an employer "causes" an employee to go without a day of rest, within the meaning of section 552, when it induces the employee to forgo rest to which the employee is entitled; an employer is not forbidden from permitting or allowing an employee, fully apprised of the entitlement to rest, to independently choose not to take a day of rest.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-03]
  "1. A day of rest is guaranteed for each workweek. Periods of more than six consecutive days of work that stretch across more than one workweek are not per se prohibited. 2. The exemption for employees working shifts of six hours or less applies only to those who never exceed six hours of work on any day of the workweek. If on any one day an employee works more than six hours, a day of rest must be provided during that workweek, subject to whatever other exceptions might apply. 3. An employer causes its employee to go without a day of rest when it induces the employee to forgo rest to which he or she is entitled. An employer is not, however, forbidden from permitting or allowing an employee, fully apprised of the entitlement to rest, independently to choose not to take a day of rest."
  — Mendoza v. Nordstrom, Inc. (2017) 2 Cal.5th 1074, California Supreme Court, construing Labor Code §§ 551, 552, and 556 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/4389644/mendoza-v-nordstrom-inc/)
  Known gap: This is a California Supreme Court decision construing California statutes discussed elsewhere in this information sheet (Labor Code §§ 551, 552, 556); it is a different kind of source from those statutes (case law rather than enacted text) and is independent of them, though it directly interprets their wording rather than addressing a separate legal question. The case arose on certified questions from a federal appellate case (a Private Attorneys General Act action against a specific retail employer), and the summary above states the court's own numbered answers to the certified questions as the court wrote them; it does not address every fact-specific application the opinion discusses, such as how the "cause" standard applies to any particular scheduling practice.

ACKNOWLEDGMENT
By signing below, the undersigned acknowledge that this information sheet was provided and that it states general rules of California law about the day-of-rest statutes (Labor Code §§ 551, 552, 554, and 556) and their judicial construction, rather than advice about Jordan Lee's specific schedule or Acme, Inc.'s specific scheduling practices or legal obligations.
